title: Allahu akbar
hookLine: hands raised, the prayer opens, the world is set behind you

cards: You're washed, facing the right way, and the time has come in. You're standing on a clean spot, your phone still buzzing in your pocket, half your mind on an email you didn't finish.
Then the person in front raises both hands, palms forward, up by the ears, and says two words. For the next few minutes, the email doesn't exist. You can't answer the phone.
You can't turn to chat. Something has closed behind you like a door.

teach.b: The words are Allahu akbar, and saying them is called takbir. Most people translate them as God is great. But akbar is a comparative, like bigger or greater, so a closer sense is: God is greater.
Greater than what? The sentence doesn't say, and that's the point. Greater than the email, the worry, whatever you walked in carrying.
Greater than anything you could put at the end of the sentence.
The first takbir of the prayer has its own name: takbirat al-ihram, the takbir of making things forbidden. Ihram is the same word used for a pilgrim's sacred state.
Once it's said, ordinary things become off-limits: eating, talking, looking around, anything that isn't the prayer.
A hadith in the Sunan collections puts the whole prayer in one sentence: its key is purity, its opening is the takbir, and its closing is the salam.
So the cleanness from day ninety-eight is the key, and today's words turn it. Then the hands.
Most Muslims raise them to the shoulders or to the ears; the schools of law describe it a little differently, and all of them are doing the same thing.
Many teachers describe it as throwing the world behind you.
And takbir doesn't stay in the prayer. It's in the call to prayer, it's said when a baby is born, on the Eid mornings, on a hilltop.
It marks every change of position in the prayer, as you'll hear over the next few days: the hinge the whole prayer turns on.

how: Every Muslim prayer opens with the takbir: raising the hands to the shoulders or ears and saying Allahu akbar, after which the worshipper stays focused on the prayer, not speaking, eating or turning away, until the closing salam.

o: a phrase of thanks said when something good happens
a blessing said over food before you eat
saying God is greater, the words that open prayer

games.q: what's inside the takbir — tap the pairs.

s: Allahu akbar means exactly God is great
akbar is a comparative: God is greater, with the end of the sentence left open.
after the first takbir, talking and eating are off-limits until the prayer ends
that's why it's called the takbir of making things forbidden.
every school of law raises the hands in exactly the same way
the schools describe it a little differently, to the shoulders or to the ears.

games.q: the hadith says the prayer has a key, an opening and a closing. the opening is the takbir. what is the key?
games.why: its key is purity, its opening is the takbir, and its closing is the salam. the cleanness from day 98 is the key.

practice: Stand, if you can, and think of the one thing tugging at you most right now; name it silently.
Then raise both hands, palms forward, to your shoulders or your ears, and if you pray, say it once, quietly, Allahu akbar; if not, just notice the feeling of setting something behind you.
Lower your hands, and let the next two minutes be empty of that thing.

wordCard.voice: Takbir. Saying Allahu akbar, God is greater: the opening of the prayer, the door that closes behind you. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: God is greater. takbir (تَكْبِير) is the act of saying it.

carryVoice: Your line: greater than all of it. Whatever feels like the biggest thing in the room, the sentence stays open. That's day one hundred one.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 61; Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3 (its key is purity, its opening the takbir, its closing the taslim)
Sahih al-Bukhari 735–739 (raising the hands with the takbir)
